In today's conference call, Tim Cook discussed Apple's increasingly severe memory supply and pricing pressures, but hinted that adding more suppliers may not bring product prices back down. Here are the details.

"Pricing remains uncertain"

Apple is seeking solutions to alleviate the memory shortage (which has forced Apple to raise prices on multiple products) and has been actively lobbying the U.S. government publicly and behind the scenes to approve the procurement of memory from Chinese suppliers ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) and Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC), both of which are on the entity list.

During today's Q3 FY2026 earnings conference call, Tim Cook and Apple CFO Kevan Parekh were asked whether Apple's push to diversify its memory supply "is meant to ensure supply stability and hedge against memory price hikes, or whether it places greater emphasis on maintaining value positioning for customers."

After outlining the sharp rise in Apple's memory costs over the past few quarters, Cook said that adding suppliers would help improve the supply situation, but also warned that this would not necessarily allow Apple to reverse its recent product price increases:

It is worth noting that Cook initially hinted that adding suppliers might help lower prices, but then deliberately corrected himself—possibly to avoid raising expectations too high.

It is worth mentioning that, according to reports, Apple plans to use memory from Chinese suppliers in products sold outside the U.S. Even so, this should help Apple prioritize allocating components from its existing suppliers to products sold in the U.S. market, thereby improving supply in both the domestic U.S. and overseas markets.

In any case, Cook's second clarification on "what adding suppliers actually means" clearly indicates that recent (and potentially future) price increases may not be just a temporary measure, as many consumers had hoped.
